  "text": "Maren leveled the iron gaff hook at the figure’s breastplate, though her boots were slipping on the silt-slicked stones. "Stay back. What are you?"

The diver stepped fully into the entryway, lead-soled boots thudding like anvils. As she cleared the knee-deep surge, water did not drain from the canvas suit; instead, Maren saw dark brine sloshing *inside* the glass faceplate, submerging the pale woman’s chin. Delicate, crimson-lined slits pulsed along her neck.

"A Sinker," the collarbone grille buzzed, the sound wet and metallic. "A warden of the low weights. A trench-shear tore the plumb-line from my harness three leagues down. I followed its ticking up the shelf, only to find a dry-lander winding the release gear."

"The spire in the trench," Maren said, remembering the amber light upstairs. "It’s displacing the sea."

"It is the Counter-Tide Engine," the Sinker rasped, leaning heavily against the curving masonry as the suit’s internal water weighed her down in the air. "It keeps the crust pinned and the deep vents capped. By turning the screw, you told the Engine the sky had fallen. Now it rises to meet the zenith."

A low, sub-audible tremor vibrated through the tower's granite foundation, shaking rust from the spiral stairs. Outside, a wave broke against the stone ten feet higher than the equinoctial mark.

"If I turn the screw back?" Maren asked.

"The brass has only the weight of a hand-lamp on its own," the Sinker said, pointing a dripping gauntlet toward the ceiling. "To drive the Engine down, we must set the plumb-line inside your great lens. It must shine across the whole bay.""
}

  "text": ""That’s ninety steps of cast iron," Maren said, eyeing the bloated canvas limbs and the lead corselet. "You’ll tear the treads from the wall."

"Then haul, dry-lander," the Sinker buzzed, gripping the central column with a bronze-gloved hand. "Or breathe silt with me when the roof goes under."

The climb was a slow agony of groaning iron and sloshing brine. Every step required Maren to brace her shoulder beneath the Sinker’s cold, dripping elbow, taking half the crushing deadweight of the trapped sea. Behind them, the Atlantic climbed the stairwell like a hunting hound, warm foam licking at their heels as the tower’s lower windows blew inward with muffled thuds.

When they finally lurched into the watch room, the amber projection was blazing like a furnace. The glowing bathymetric lines were stretched taut, and the geometric spire had pierced the plane of the table entirely, its phantom apex skewering the ceiling planks.

Outside the rain-lashed glass, a mile off the point, the black surface of the bay split open.

A monolithic point of basalt and glowing bronze ribs rose through the boiling surf, shedding cataracts of steaming water. The displaced swell hit the headland seconds later, a solid wall of white water that buried the keeper’s cottage and made the whole granite tower sway like a mast.

Maren snatched the ticking armillary sphere from the chart table, its rings spinning fast enough to blur. "The lantern room is just above. If we put this in the focal plane, what happens to the oil lamp?"

"Snuff it," the Sinker rasped, bubbles frothing past her crimson gills as she reached for the steep ladder hatch. "Light of tallow cannot push iron. Only the heavy spectrum.""

Outside, the dense beam swept across the boiling bay and struck the basalt spire’s peak. 

The roar of the Engine fractured into a deafening metallic shriek. The monolith shuddered, its upward climb halting as millions of tons of magnified downward force pinned it like an insect.

The violet beam flared blindingly white. Out in the bay, the spire plummeted into the abyss like a dropped guillotine blade. Gravity snapped back instantly, slamming Maren and the Sinker hard against the iron grating."
